## Learning Objectives {-}

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

- Apply fundamental dimensioning rules according to ASME Y14.5 standards
- Select appropriate dimension placement for clarity and manufacturability
- Use proper extension lines, dimension lines, and leaders
- Dimension common features including holes, arcs, and angles
- Avoid common dimensioning errors

::: {.callout-think}
**Before You Read:** Look at any mechanical part near you. How would you
communicate its exact size to someone who needs to manufacture it? What
measurements would be most important?
:::

## Introduction to Dimensioning

Dimensioning is the process of adding size and location information to
engineering drawings. Proper dimensioning ensures that parts can be
manufactured exactly as the designer intended.

::: {.callout-industry}
**Industry Connection:** NASA's Mars Climate Orbiter was lost in 1999 because one team's software
reported thruster impulse in pound-force seconds while the navigation software expected
newton seconds. The same kind of unit mix-up happens on drawings: a dimension of 25 means
something very different in millimetres and in inches. Stating the units, and following one set
of dimensioning rules, prevents such costly mistakes.
:::

## Elements of a Dimension

A dimension is made of a few standard line types, all drawn thin so that they do not compete with the visible outline of the part:

* **Extension lines** carry a feature out of the view. They start with a small visible **gap** (about 1.5 mm) from the part and run about **3 mm past** the last dimension line.
* **Dimension lines** run between the extension lines and end in **arrowheads** that touch the extension lines. The number sits in a break in the line (ASME) or above it (ISO).
* **Leaders** connect a note or a size callout to a feature. A leader to a hole or arc is drawn radially, so that if extended it would pass through the **centre**. It starts with a short horizontal shoulder at the note.
* **Centre lines** (long–short dashes) mark the axis of holes and cylinders. A centre line may be extended and used as an extension line; it does not need a gap.

```{r fig-dimension-elements, echo=FALSE, fig.width=9, fig.height=5.6, fig.align='center', fig.cap="Elements of a dimension on a plate with one hole (mm): extension lines start with a small gap from the part and run a little past the dimension line; smaller dimensions sit closer to the part; the hole is located at its centre and sized with a leader in its circular view."}
## Plate 80 x 50 with a Ø12 hole located 20 from the left edge and 25 from the bottom edge
circ <- function(cx, cy, r, n = 120) { a <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = n); data.frame(x = cx + r * cos(a), y = cy + r * sin(a)) }
hc <- c(20, 25); hr <- 6
gap <- 1.5; over <- 3
arw <- arrow(length = unit(0.16, "cm"), ends = "both", type = "closed")
arw1 <- arrow(length = unit(0.16, "cm"), type = "closed")
lab_col <- "firebrick"
ts <- 3.6 * diagram_text_scale
ls <- 3.0 * diagram_text_scale
## leader: radial line at 45 degrees that ends on the hole edge
a45 <- pi / 4
tip <- hc + hr * c(cos(a45), sin(a45))
kne <- hc + 42 * c(cos(a45), sin(a45))

ggplot() +
  ## part outline and hole
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = 0, xmax = 80, ymin = 0, ymax = 50), fill = "white", color = "black", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_path(data = circ(hc[1], hc[2], hr), aes(x, y), color = "black", linewidth = 1) +
  ## centre lines (the vertical one is extended to serve as an extension line)
  geom_segment(aes(x = hc[1], xend = hc[1], y = hc[2] + hr + 3, yend = -10 - over), linetype = "F282", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = hc[1] + hr + 3, xend = -10 - over, y = hc[2], yend = hc[2]), linetype = "F282", linewidth = 0.35) +
  ## extension lines (gap at the part, run "over" past the outer dimension line)
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = 0, y = -gap, yend = -20 - over), linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 80, xend = 80, y = -gap, yend = -20 - over), linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = -gap, xend = -20 - over, y = 0, yend = 0), linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = -gap, xend = -20 - over, y = 50, yend = 50), linewidth = 0.35) +
  ## dimension lines: small dimensions nearest the part, overall dimensions outside
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = 20, y = -10, yend = -10), linewidth = 0.35, arrow = arw) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = 80, y = -20, yend = -20), linewidth = 0.35, arrow = arw) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = -10, xend = -10, y = 0, yend = 25), linewidth = 0.35, arrow = arw) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = -20, xend = -20, y = 0, yend = 50), linewidth = 0.35, arrow = arw) +
  annotate("label", x = 10, y = -10, label = "20", size = ts, fill = "white", linewidth = 0) +
  annotate("label", x = 40, y = -20, label = "80", size = ts, fill = "white", linewidth = 0) +
  annotate("label", x = -10, y = 12.5, label = "25", size = ts, fill = "white", linewidth = 0) +
  annotate("label", x = -20, y = 25, label = "50", size = ts, fill = "white", linewidth = 0) +
  ## leader with a short horizontal shoulder and the diameter note
  geom_segment(aes(x = kne[1], xend = tip[1], y = kne[2], yend = tip[2]), linewidth = 0.35, arrow = arw1) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = kne[1], xend = kne[1] + 5, y = kne[2], yend = kne[2]), linewidth = 0.35) +
  annotate("text", x = kne[1] + 6, y = kne[2], label = "Ø12", hjust = 0, size = ts) +

  ## ---- names of the elements (red) ----
  annotate("text", x = 108, y = 60, label = "Leader\n(points at the centre)", color = lab_col, size = ls, fontface = "italic") +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 97, xend = 42, y = 57, yend = 46.6), color = lab_col, linewidth = 0.4, arrow = arw1) +
  annotate("text", x = 108, y = 22, label = "Extension line", color = lab_col, size = ls, fontface = "italic") +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 98, xend = 80.7, y = 20, yend = -6), color = lab_col, linewidth = 0.4, arrow = arw1) +
  annotate("text", x = 108, y = 5, label = "Visible gap\nat the part", color = lab_col, size = ls, fontface = "italic") +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 98, xend = 81.2, y = 1, yend = -0.8), color = lab_col, linewidth = 0.4, arrow = arw1) +
  annotate("text", x = 108, y = -28, label = "Dimension line\nwith arrowheads", color = lab_col, size = ls, fontface = "italic") +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 96, xend = 62, y = -26, yend = -20.6), color = lab_col, linewidth = 0.4, arrow = arw1) +
  annotate("text", x = 50, y = -33, label = "Extends ~3 mm past\nthe dimension line", color = lab_col, size = ls, fontface = "italic") +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 66, xend = 79, y = -31, yend = -22.5), color = lab_col, linewidth = 0.4, arrow = arw1) +
  annotate("text", x = -32, y = 62, label = "Centre line", color = lab_col, size = ls, fontface = "italic") +
  geom_segment(aes(x = -24, xend = 19.5, y = 60, yend = 33), color = lab_col, linewidth = 0.4, arrow = arw1) +
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = -33, label = "Centre line used\nas extension line", color = lab_col, size = ls, fontface = "italic") +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 8, xend = 19.5, y = -30, yend = -12), color = lab_col, linewidth = 0.4, arrow = arw1) +

  coord_fixed(xlim = c(-45, 122), ylim = c(-38, 68)) +
  labs(title = "Elements of a Dimension") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5))
```

## Basic Dimensioning Rules (ASME Y14.5)

1. **Dimension each feature once.** A dimension repeated in a second view will contradict the first one the day only one of them is revised.
2. **Do not over-dimension.** In a chain of dimensions whose total is also given, leave one link out, or show it in parentheses as a *reference dimension*; otherwise the tolerances cannot all be met at once.
3. **Dimension in the view that shows the shape most clearly** (the characteristic view): a hole's diameter in the view where it appears as a circle, a slot's width where its outline is seen.
4. **Never dimension to hidden lines.** Use a visible edge, or add a section view that makes the feature visible.
5. **Place dimensions outside the view** where possible, with the **smaller dimensions closest to the part** and the larger ones outside them. Then extension lines never cross dimension lines.
6. **Dimension lines should not cross** each other or other lines. Extension lines may cross each other and visible lines when there is no other way.
7. **Locate holes by their centres**, not by their edges, and give their size with a diameter symbol: Ø12. Arcs are sized with a radius: R8.
8. **Choose dimensions from the part's function.** Measure from the surfaces that locate the part in the assembly (later, its datums), not from whatever edge was convenient to draw.
9. **State the units.** A drawing is all millimetres or all inches, with a note in the title block. Metric values below 1 get a leading zero (0.5, not .5); inch values drop it (.50). The full zero and decimal-place rules are in the Tolerances chapter.
10. **Use standard symbols and abbreviations** (Ø, R, ⌴ counterbore, ⌵ countersink, ↧ depth) so that anyone can read the drawing.

## Try it yourself {#sec-tryit-dimensioning}

```{r tryit-dim-sort, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
tryit_sort(
  id = "dimension-practice",
  title = "Good practice or a dimensioning error?",
  bins = c("Good practice", "Dimensioning error"),
  cards = data.frame(
    text = c(
      "Each dimension is stated once on the drawing",
      "The same hole diameter is dimensioned in both the front view and the top view",
      "A dimension is placed on the view that shows the feature's shape most clearly",
      "A dimension is given to a hidden line instead of to a visible edge",
      "Dimensions are chosen to relate to the function of the part",
      "Numbers are given without units in a drawing that mixes inch and metric values and has no note",
      "Standard symbols and conventions are used so that anyone can read the drawing",
      "Several dimensions cross one another in a crowded view where space was available elsewhere"
    ),
    bin = c("Good practice", "Dimensioning error", "Good practice", "Dimensioning error",
            "Good practice", "Dimensioning error", "Good practice", "Dimensioning error"),
    why = c(
      "Repeating a dimension invites contradictions when the drawing is revised.",
      "A dimension should appear only once.",
      "Placement should be for maximum clarity.",
      "Do not dimension to hidden lines; use a visible edge or a section.",
      "Dimensions should relate to functional requirements.",
      "Unit confusion is how the Mars Climate Orbiter was lost.",
      "Standard symbols give universal understanding.",
      "Dimensions should be placed for clarity; crossing lines hide meaning."
    )
  ),
  intro = "Decide whether each practice follows the chapter's dimensioning rules.",
  question = "<p>Classify each practice as good dimensioning practice or a dimensioning error, using the rules of this chapter.</p>"
)
```

## Key Takeaways {-}

- Dimensions should be placed for maximum clarity
- Each dimension should appear only once on a drawing
- Dimensions should relate to functional requirements
- Standard symbols and conventions ensure universal understanding

::: {.callout-check}
**Quick Check:** What is the difference between an extension line and a
dimension line? Why is it important not to dimension to hidden lines?
:::
